q: Every rum in the world begins with which raw material?
exp: Most of the Caribbean ferments molasses, the residue of sugar refining. Rhum agricole, the Martinique style, ferments fresh-pressed cane juice instead and tastes grassier for it.

q: Brazil's national spirit is pressed and fermented from cane on the day it is cut. What is it called?
exp: Cachaca is legally its own category in Brazil rather than a rum, and it is the base of the caipirinha. Unaged versions are clear; aged ones rest in native woods.

q: Which botanical has to lead for a spirit to be sold as gin at all?
exp: Juniper must be the predominant flavour by law. Coriander, angelica and orris are common supporting players but none of them can carry the category.

q: No flavouring or colouring may be introduced once the spirit has left the still. Which style carries that restriction?
exp: London Dry is a method rather than a place, so it can be made anywhere. Old Tom is sweetened, genever is built on malt wine, and sloe gin is a flavoured liqueur.

q: Rectifying a spirit to a very high strength and stripping out what character remains produces which category?
exp: The base can be grain, potato, grape or molasses, since the aim of the process is to remove its fingerprint. The other three are all deliberately flavoured after or during distillation.

q: A bitter red Italian aperitivo, taken with soda or in a Negroni, is most likely which of these?
exp: A Negroni is equal parts gin, Campari and sweet vermouth. Fernet is a bracing digestive, Cynar is built on artichoke, and Averna is sweeter and darker.

q: Which category covers the bitter Italian herbal digestives poured after a meal?
exp: Amaro simply means bitter, and the family runs from gentle to punishing. Amaretto is sweet and almond-scented, sambuca is anise-led, and limoncello is a lemon liqueur.

q: Green and yellow versions of one French herbal liqueur have been produced by Carthusian monks for centuries. Which is it?
exp: The green is the stronger and more assertive of the pair, the yellow softer and honeyed. The recipe draws on a long list of botanicals and has never been published.

q: Aniseed-scented spirits turn milky white the moment water is added. What is that effect called?
exp: Anethole dissolves in alcohol but not in water, so it drops out of solution as an emulsion. Pastis, ouzo, raki and absinthe all do it.

q: Strip away the romance and the ground beneath a vineyard has a short list of practical jobs to do. Which list is it?
opts: Sterilise the root zone, repel insects, suppress weeds and hold the winter snow
Set the alcohol, the aroma and the sweetness that the finished wine will show
Supply the sugar, the acid, the colour and the tannin the berry will need
Anchor the roots, hold water, release nutrients and store heat
exp: Anchorage every soil manages. What separates one site from the next is how much water is held, how much nitrogen is released and how quickly the ground warms in spring, and those three between them govern the size of the vine and the size of its crop.

q: Puddles stand in the rows for a week after every storm, and the vines there are yellow and stunted while the rest of the block looks well. What are those roots short of?
opts: Oxygen, because water has filled the air spaces between the soil particles
Light, because none of it can reach a root sitting under standing water
Potassium, because that nutrient is released only from a dry soil
Nitrogen, because the standing water has washed it down out of reach
exp: Roots breathe, and they take their oxygen from the pores between soil particles. Fill those with water for long enough and a root suffocates and rots, which is why free drainage is the first thing anyone assessing a site looks for, and why heavy ground is so often drained before a vine is planted in it.

q: A grower calls his best parcel poor ground and plainly means it as praise. What is he saying about the soil?
opts: It was cheap land that none of his neighbours wanted to farm
It has been worn out by several generations of continuous cropping
It is short of nutrients and water, so the vine cannot grow rank
It is far too acidic for any crop other than a vine to tolerate
exp: Give a vine plenty of water and nitrogen and it spends them on shoots and leaves, shading its own fruit and diluting it into the bargain. Hunger at the root is why so many celebrated vineyards sit on ground a farmer would refuse for any other crop.

q: A trench dug across a vineyard exposes thirty centimetres of dark crumbly earth, then two metres of stony clay, then rock. Which of those layers is doing most for a mature vine in a rainless August?
opts: None of them, since by August a mature vine is living on what its leaves make
The stony clay, since that is where the older roots and the last of the water are
The rock, since a mature root system dissolves it for the minerals it holds
The dark surface earth, since that is the layer holding most of the nutrients
exp: A young vine lives in the top layer; an established one has roots metres down and takes its late-summer water from the subsoil. That is why a soil is judged by digging a pit rather than by scraping the surface, and why two blocks with identical topsoil can behave nothing alike.

q: Six rainless weeks arrive, and two blocks of the same age and variety face them, one over half a metre of soil on hard rock and one over three metres. Which suffers first?
opts: The deep block, because its roots are kept closer to the hot surface
Neither of them, because the depth of a soil has no bearing on drought
The deep block, because roots that have gone down deep dry out faster
The shallow block, because a thin soil holds a much smaller reserve of water
exp: How much water a vineyard can store comes down to how much soil the roots can reach. A thin skin of earth over impermeable rock empties first, and the danger is not thirst in September but a block that has already run dry in July with the fruit still green.

q: Water tipped onto this ground disappears at once, it grates between finger and thumb, and it keeps almost nothing back for the vine. Which soil is it?
exp: Sand grains are large, so the gaps between them are large and gravity empties them within hours. A vine on pure sand depends on rain or irrigation because nothing is held in reserve, and the wines that come off it tend to be pale, perfumed and light in tannin.

q: Squeezed in the palm it rolls into a ribbon without breaking, it is still damp a fortnight after rain, and by August it has set hard and cracked open. Name that soil.
exp: Clay particles are microscopically small and flat, so they pack close together, grip water hard and grip nutrients with it. That reserve is worth a great deal in a dry region and is a liability in a wet one, where the vine's feet are never dry.
